power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

info.title: Beyond Behavioral Adaptation: Evaluating the Added Value of EEG in Personalized Language Interfaces

author.affiliation:
Faculty of Psychology and Education Sciences
								University of Coimbra

Faculty of Psychology and Education Sciences
								University of Coimbra

Faculty of Psychology and Education Sciences
								University of Coimbra

text.text: Neuroadaptive interfaces personalize human-computer interaction using brain activity, but whether neural measurements provide useful information beyond behavioral indicators remains unclear, particularly in language comprehension tasks.
We propose a framework to investigate the added value of EEG in adaptive communication support.
Written messages are presented through combinations of sentence segmentation, pictograms, and keyword labels, with presentation choices informed by individual preferences and task performance.
A behavior-adaptive policy serves as the baseline for comparison with a neuroadaptive policy incorporating calibrated EEG estimates under signal-quality and uncertainty constraints.
The research plan includes interface validation, behavioral feasibility testing, and an EEGbased comparison using held-out sessions.
Evaluation focuses on comprehension accuracy, response time, subjective effort, and adaptation behavior.
The objective is to determine whether neural information improves assistance decisions and user outcomes beyond behavioral adaptation.
Communication technologies have made substantial progress in overcoming limitations of conventional speech and motor output.

Intracranial speech brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) have demonstrated rapid text decoding and multimodal speechrelated output in individual participants with severe paralysis [1], [2], [3], [4], [5], [5], [6], [7], [8].
text.formatted: Intracranial speech brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) have demonstrated rapid text decoding and multimodal speechrelated output in individual participants with severe paralysis <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">[1]</ref>, <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">[2]</ref>, <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[3]</ref>, <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">[4]</ref>, <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">[5]</ref>, <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">[5]</ref>, <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">[6]</ref>, <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">[7]</ref>, <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">[8]</ref>.

text.text: At the same time, clinical translation still raises questions of robustness, training, longterm use, and the division of learning between users and decoders [9].
text.formatted: At the same time, clinical translation still raises questions of robustness, training, longterm use, and the division of learning between users and decoders <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">[9]</ref>.

text.text: Non-invasive speech decoding research addresses a different point on the feasibility spectrum as many studies tried decoding different aspects of speech [10], [11], [12], [13].
text.formatted: Non-invasive speech decoding research addresses a different point on the feasibility spectrum as many studies tried decoding different aspects of speech <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">[10]</ref>, <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">[11]</ref>, <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">[12]</ref>, <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">[13]</ref>.

text.text: Such demonstrations are important steps toward neural access to communication, but they should not be confused with readyto-use, open-vocabulary communication systems.
Access, however, is only one part of a successful interaction.
Once a message is available, a person still needs to understand, formulate, or select it.
The relevant difficulties vary widely across acquired motor impairments, language disorders, and developmental conditions; these are not interchangeable clinical populations.

Even within a single population, identical presentations may place different demands on perception, language, and working memory, as is the case for attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), dyslexia, and autism per example [14], [15], [16].
text.formatted: Even within a single population, identical presentations may place different demands on perception, language, and working memory, as is the case for attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), dyslexia, and autism per example <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">[14]</ref>, <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">[15]</ref>, <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">[16]</ref>.

text.text: This does not establish an neural marker of comprehension, but it illustrates why a diagnosis alone is an incomplete specification of an individual's languageprocessing profile.
Adaptive presentation offers one possible response.

In a small supervised study involving learners with special educational needs, sentence segmentation and pictorial scaffolds did not produce a uniform pattern of benefit; richer displays could also introduce coordination costs [17].
text.formatted: In a small supervised study involving learners with special educational needs, sentence segmentation and pictorial scaffolds did not produce a uniform pattern of benefit; richer displays could also introduce coordination costs <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">[17]</ref>.

text.text: Meanwhile, automated mapping of textual concepts to pictograms has shown the technical feasibility of generating such supports across several languages, although languagespecific repository coverage and semantic ambiguity remain relevant [18].
text.formatted: Meanwhile, automated mapping of textual concepts to pictograms has shown the technical feasibility of generating such supports across several languages, although languagespecific repository coverage and semantic ambiguity remain relevant <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">[18]</ref>.

text.text: Thus, the ability to generate support and the decision to use it are separate problems.
Neuroadaptive systems extend adaptive interaction by using brain activity to inform the interface, typically through passive estimates of an aspect of the user's state [19], [20].
text.formatted: Neuroadaptive systems extend adaptive interaction by using brain activity to inform the interface, typically through passive estimates of an aspect of the user's state <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">[19]</ref>, <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">[20]</ref>.

text.text: Recent EEG-informed conversational systems have demonstrated adaptive text generation, but improvements in engagement did not necessarily translate into improved learning outcomes [21].
text.formatted: Recent EEG-informed conversational systems have demonstrated adaptive text generation, but improvements in engagement did not necessarily translate into improved learning outcomes <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">[21]</ref>.

text.text: This motivates a more circumscribed question in communication support: when, if ever, does neural information improve the choice of a linguistic aid beyond what can be inferred from behavior?
We outline a project to answer this question.
Its contribution is not a new speech decoder or a claim of clinical efficacy.

It is a modular distinction between communication access, support selection, and the evidence used for adaptation, accompanied by an evaluation designed to isolate the added value of neural measurements.
The proposed interface is organized around a message, a user model, and a constrained adaptation policy (Fig. 1).
text.formatted: The proposed interface is organized around a message, a user model, and a constrained adaptation policy (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>).

text.text: The message can arrive through ordinary text input, speech recognition, or an alternative access method.
Neural speech decoding is a possible longer-term input route, not a prerequisite for the initial experiments.

Crucially, the neural activity used to decode an intended message and the neural activity used to estimate cognitive state serve different functions, require different validation, and need not be measured with the same system.

For the first prototype, a message is presented in one of four controlled formats: unmodified text; sentence-segmented text; segmented text with selected pictograms; or the latter with keyword labels.
These conditions are deliberately close to previously studied scaffolds [17], allowing the work to concentrate on selection rather than on inventing new forms of assistance.
text.formatted: These conditions are deliberately close to previously studied scaffolds <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">[17]</ref>, allowing the work to concentrate on selection rather than on inventing new forms of assistance.

text.text: Optional read-aloud output can be added in a later version.
The underlying wording is held constant between the four initial formats, so that changes in performance are not attributed to simultaneous, uncontrolled text rewriting.
The user model has two timescales.
A slowly updated profile summarizes language assessments, preferred formats, and accessibility settings.
A task-level record contains correctness, response time, requests for help, and recent selections.
Neural information, if collected, enters as a calibrated estimate with an explicit measure of uncertainty.
It does not determine whether a response has been understood.
Let aₜ denote the presentation format selected for the next item and hₜ the available behavioral history.
A behavioradaptive policy chooses aₜ from hₜ and the user's stated constraints.
Its neuroadaptive counterpart additionally uses a neural estimate ẑₜ only if signal quality and calibration criteria are satisfied.
Both policies have the same set of actions and are trained under the same information budget.
A low-confidence neural estimate triggers the behavioral policy rather than an enforced interface change.
To avoid disruptive fluctuations, adaptation initially occurs between messages, not during the reading of a sentence.
Users and clinicians can override any selection.
We favor an interpretable, regularized policy over unconstrained reinforcement learning at this stage.

A small feasibility sample will not support complex individual policies, and the system must remain auditable: its choice should be traceable to recent performance, preferences, or a properly validated neural estimate.
An initial prototype will implement the four presentation formats and log the timing and source of every adaptation.
French and Spanish are suitable first languages for a controlled pilot; extension to other languages will depend on content coverage and qualified review.
Automatically selected pictograms will be checked for semantic adequacy, polysemy, and unintended changes in meaning.
Stimuli will be short functional messages and brief passages with comprehension questions, not arbitrary generated text.
A small group of speechlanguage and accessibility professionals will review materials before participant testing.
We envisage a pilot of approximately 30 adults covering a range of reading and language abilities, including a subgroup reporting developmental reading difficulties.
The number is a feasibility target, not a power calculation or a claim that data have been collected.
Clinical diagnoses, if used for subgroup analyses, will be verified rather than inferred from performance.
Eligibility and accessible testing procedures will be finalized with clinical collaborators and ethics approval.
Participants will encounter equivalent, counterbalanced sets of messages under a fixed-format interface and a behavioradaptive interface.
A short calibration block will estimate baseline performance and preferences.
The adaptive rule will then be locked for evaluation on held-out messages, avoiding an overly optimistic assessment on the same material used to tune it.
Different message sets, rather than repetitions of the same questions, will be used across conditions.
The initial objective is to estimate feasibility, within-person variability, adherence, and effect-size uncertainty; a larger, separately powered study would be needed for efficacy claims.
In a subsequent EEG-equipped subset, the same tasks will compare the fixed condition, the behavior-adaptive policy, and the identical policy supplemented by EEG-derived information.
A separate calibration task will be used to test whether the chosen EEG features capture a reproducible state relevant to the task.
Spectral measures may be considered, but no single frequency band will be presumed to measure comprehension.
Artifacts, eye movements, and changes in visual layout must be addressed because they can correlate with both the selected scaffold and the neural features.
Incremental value will be tested on held-out sessions.
A neural-label permutation control will help identify apparent gains caused by chance or model complexity; signal-quality failures and missing data will be reported rather than selectively excluded.
The comparison is meaningful only if neural measurements change decisions and those changes improve user outcomes.
Accurate decoding of a surrogate EEG label, by itself, will not meet that criterion.
The primary behavioral outcome will be comprehension accuracy, accompanied by response time to characterize the speed-accuracy trade-off.
Prespecified secondary measures will include subjective effort, requests for assistance, adaptation frequency, overrides, interface latency, and semantic errors in pictogram selection.
Communication rate may become relevant for a later message-composition or BCI-access task, but should not substitute for comprehension in the proposed first study.
Analyses will compare policies within participant while accounting for repeated items; mixed-effects models and effect estimates with uncertainty intervals are appropriate starting points.
Any group-by-policy interaction in the pilot will be treated as exploratory.
For the neural condition, a positive result would require improvement over the behavior-adaptive comparator, not merely over a static display.
Conversely, no added neural benefit would be informative: it would indicate that the cost and complexity of EEG are not justified for this task under the tested conditions.
Several boundaries are important.
Neither a languageprocessing difference observed in dyslexia nor a neural workload estimate can automatically be generalized to people living with locked-in syndrome.
The initial prototype addresses support selection for language comprehension; integrating an implantable speech decoder would constitute a separate clinical development and validation effort.
Adaptation also creates risks of excessive assistance, unstable display changes, and reduced user agency.
We therefore constrain permissible changes, preserve manual control, and treat language-specific content safety and data privacy as prerequisites, not secondary refinements.
The project proposes a testable route from generic assistive communication toward personalization informed by individual behavior and, where justified, neural state.
Its main premise is deliberately conditional: neural measurements should be added only when they provide reliable information that improves the user's actual communication outcome.

This separation of access, adaptation, and evaluation makes it possible to build on progress in speech BCIs and multilingual language support without assuming that their integration is already clinically effective.
Figure 1: Proposed separation of message access, state estimation, and selection of language support.
The neural branch is optional and is tested against the behavioral branch alone.
The figure describes a planned system, not an implemented clinical device.
